description: Potosí's silver mines, the mita labor draft, and the price revolution — how one Andean mountain wired the first global economy.
essential_question: How did one mountain of silver wire the first global economy?

key_terms.definition: The Andean silver-mining center whose output bankrolled Spain's empire after 1545.
The Spanish colonial labor draft, adapted from the Inca mit'a, requiring Indigenous communities to send workers to the mines.
The century-long rise of European prices, roughly tripling by 1600, driven by the flood of American silver.

learning_objectives: Describe how the mita draft supplied labor for Potosí's silver mines.
Explain the price revolution as an effect of American silver in Europe.
Trace silver's path from Potosí to the Manila galleons and the global economy.

presentation.tone: a teacher talking to a smart 16-year-old; plain, spoken, concrete

narration.text: [beat]High in the Andes sits a mountain the Spanish called Cerro Rico, the Rich Hill. In [date:1545] they struck silver there, and the city below it swelled to two hundred thousand people, as large as London. [beat] The workers called it something else: the mountain that eats men. [awed]This is the story of how one mountain wired the first global economy. How did one mountain rewire the world's economy, and what did it cost?

scenes.production_notes: Question hook: the mountain is established, then the lesson's framing question is asked outright (how did one mountain rewire the world's economy?). It is answered in s4. Low wind drone; silence under 'the mountain that eats men.' Fallback: if the mountain composition fails, a high-altitude mining settlement with tiny figures.

The story goes that in [date:1545], an Andean herder named Diego Huallpa was chasing lost llamas on Cerro Rico. He built a fire against the cold, and the ground beneath it melted into shining liquid. Silver. [beat] Within years, Potosí was producing most of the world's silver. But Spain had a problem. The mountain was rich, and there was almost no one to dig it.

narration.text: Spain's answer was the mita. The Inca had used a labor draft called the mit'a for roads and terraces, taking turns from each village. In [date:1573], the viceroy Francisco de Toledo repurposed it for the mines. [beat] Here is the order, read as it was written. Then listen to a man who lived under it.

scenes.production_notes: The law looks legitimate here, warm and orderly, so the mitayo's testimony cuts deeper. The host introduces both voices in this scene (decree, then mitayo). Fallback: a close detail of the wax seal and quill.

narration.text: [VOICE:mitayo][solemn]They took us from our villages to the cold mountain. We climbed down on rope ladders, candles tied to our thumbs. We crushed ore with our hands and breathed the mercury smoke. [beat] The wage could not buy back our health. Many never came home.

The voice reads the image like a document. Coordinates must be tuned against the actual plate at animatic stage. narration.text: [beat]The silver came out through poison. Miners mixed crushed ore with mercury on open patios, treading it barefoot. The mercury grabbed the silver, and heat burned the mercury away as vapor. [solemn]It worked on low-grade ore the old smelters could not touch, which is why Potosí kept producing for two centuries. It also poisoned everyone who touched it.

scenes.production_notes: Harsh daylight. The poisoning lands flat, without melodrama. Fallback: a close detail of hands mixing amalgam in a stone basin.

beats.cue: Historians call it the price revolution

narration.text: All that silver crossed the Atlantic to Spain, and then it kept going. More money chasing the same goods meant prices climbed across Europe for a hundred years. By 1600, prices were three to four times higher than in 1500. [beat] Historians call it the price revolution, and it was the first great inflation of the modern world.

scenes.production_notes: Slow pull-back as the scale widens from Spain to Europe. The 'more money chasing the same goods' line is the mechanism; say it plainly. Fallback: a tight detail of stacked silver bars and a merchant's scale.

narration.text: Spain became the richest country in Europe. So Spain won? [beat] Not so fast. Spain spent the silver on wars and imported goods instead of building industry. By the end of the 1500s, the richest empire on earth had gone bankrupt four times. [wry]The silver enriched Spain's rivals more than Spain itself.

scenes.production_notes: Device: reversal pivot. 'Spain became the richest country in Europe' is the steelman, built up so 'Not so fast' lands. Locked frame; stillness is the verdict. Single low thud under the stamp; silence after. Stamp 1 of 2. Fallback: an empty strongbox with its lid thrown back.

moves.label: ACAPULCO TO MANILA

narration.text: [beat]Follow the silver, in two streams. Potosí's silver sailed east: it crossed the Atlantic to Spain. And from [date:1565], Mexican silver sailed west: the Manila galleons carried it west across the Pacific, from Acapulco to Manila, trading it for Chinese silk and porcelain. [awed]China hungered for silver to run its tax system, and as much as a third of all American silver ended up in Asia. One mountain in the Andes, wired to the whole world.

scenes.production_notes: Device: map tracing. Three arrows draw in sequence as the narration travels; each cue lands its line. Potosí's arrow runs east to Spain; the galleon arrow runs west from Acapulco to Manila: two streams, matching the narration. The hook's question (mine to world) is answered visually here. Coordinates must be tuned against the actual plate at animatic stage. Stamp 2 of 2: the stamped verdict. Gentle score swell under the final line, then fade. Fallback: if the map composition crowds, a simpler outline map of the Atlantic and Pacific with the three route arrows.
